title: Accelerating change, 1875–1905: Ehrlich, Koch and chemistry

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 3.

learn.intro: Scientists began to identify the germs behind specific diseases. Surgery moved from killing germs to keeping them out altogether, public health improved under the 1875 Act, and chemistry and physics opened new possibilities.

sections.title: 1. Koch and bacteriology

blocks.p: Robert Koch, a German doctor, proved that specific germs cause specific diseases. He identified the anthrax bacterium (1876), the tuberculosis bacterium (1882) and the cholera bacterium (1883). He developed methods to grow bacteria on solid agar and to stain them with dyes so they could be seen under a microscope.

Rivalry between France (Pasteur) and Germany (Koch) speeded up research. Pasteur developed vaccines for chicken cholera (1879), anthrax (1881) and rabies (1885), building on Edward Jenner's earlier smallpox vaccine.

evidence: 1876: anthrax; 1882: tuberculosis; 1883: cholera — all identified by Koch.

blocks.p: Antiseptic surgery killed germs with chemicals. From the 1880s surgeons moved to aseptic surgery — preventing germs from entering the wound at all. Instruments were sterilised with steam, operating theatres were cleaned thoroughly, and surgeons wore gowns, masks and caps. Rubber gloves were introduced in 1890 (by the American surgeon William Halsted).
With pain controlled by anaesthetics and infection reduced by aseptic methods, surgeons could attempt longer and more complex operations inside the body. Bleeding remained the main problem.

sections.title: 3. The impact of the Public Health Act 1875

blocks.p: Because the 1875 Act was compulsory, towns built sewers and reservoirs, provided clean water, and appointed Medical Officers of Health. Cholera epidemics ended in Britain after 1866. Death rates in towns fell, though poor housing and poverty still caused high infant mortality.

evidence: No major cholera epidemic in Britain after 1866.
Councils provided sewers and clean water under the 1875 Act.

sections.title: 4. Science and medicine: blood, magic bullets and radiation

blocks.p: Blood transfusions: early transfusions often failed because the patient's body rejected the blood. In 1901 Karl Landsteiner discovered blood groups, explaining why — though blood could not yet be stored because it clotted.

Magic bullets: Paul Ehrlich, who had worked with Koch, searched for chemicals that would kill a specific germ without harming the patient. After hundreds of tests, his team found Salvarsan 606 (1909), the first 'magic bullet', which cured syphilis.

Radioactivity: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, allowing doctors to see bones and objects inside the body. Marie Curie and Pierre Curie discovered radium and polonium in 1898; radium was used to treat cancer. Marie Curie later developed mobile X-ray units in the First World War.

flashcards.q: How did aseptic surgery change operations?
flashcards.a: Fewer infections, allowing longer and more complex operations inside the body.

flashcards.q: What was the impact of the 1875 Act?
flashcards.a: Sewers, clean water, Medical Officers; cholera epidemics ended; town death rates fell.

flashcards.q: Why did early blood transfusions often fail?
flashcards.a: Blood groups were unknown until Landsteiner (1901), so the body rejected unmatched blood.
